Core concepts

Routing

Define routes, capture :params and * wildcards, mount sub-routers, and understand exactly how a path is matched.

The route methods#

Every HTTP method has a matching method on the app (and on a Router):

js
import { createApp } from 'routiva';

const app = createApp();

app.get('/users', (req, res) => res.json([]));
app.post('/users', (req, res) => res.status(201).json(req.body));
app.put('/users/:id', replaceUser);
app.patch('/users/:id', patchUser);
app.delete('/users/:id', deleteUser);
app.head('/users/:id', headUser);
app.options('/users/:id', optionsUser);
app.all('/ping', (req, res) => res.send('pong'));
MethodRegisters
get post put patch delete head optionsA route for that one method
allA route for every method (stored with a null method)
useMiddleware (see Middleware)

A route only runs when both the path and the method match. HEAD is special: it is served by a matching GET route, with the body suppressed. See HEAD, OPTIONS and 405.

More than one handler per route#

Any number of handlers can be registered for one path. Each becomes its own layer sharing the same compiled pattern, so they run in order:

js
app.get('/reports/:id', requireAuth, loadReport, (req, res) => {
  res.json(req.report);
});

requireAuth runs first, calls next() to continue, then loadReport, then the final handler. Arrays are flattened, so app.get('/x', [a, b], c) works too. This is the same trick Express uses for route-level middleware.

Path parameters#

A :name segment captures one path segment (everything up to the next /):

js
app.get('/users/:id', (req, res) => {
  res.json({ id: req.params.id });
});
PatternRequestMatch?req.params
/users/:id/users/42✅{ id: '42' }
/users/:id/users/42/✅{ id: '42' } (trailing slash tolerated)
/users/:id/users/42/posts❌—
/users/:id/users/a%20b✅{ id: 'a b' } (decoded)
/users/:id/posts/:postId/users/7/posts/9✅{ id: '7', postId: '9' }

Captured values are URL-decoded with a safe wrapper, so a malformed escape such as %E0%A4 is left as-is instead of throwing a 500.

Params from an outer layer and an inner layer are merged, with the inner value winning. When a mounted router matches :tenant and a route inside it matches :id, the handler sees both.

text
app.use('/t/:tenant', router)      // captures { tenant }
  router.get('/u/:id', handler)    // captures { id }
                                   // handler sees { tenant, id }

routiva supports required :name segments only. Optional (:id?), inline regex (:id(\\d+)) and arrays of paths are not part of the syntax — validate inside a param() callback or the handler instead.

Wildcards#

* captures the rest of the path (including slashes) under the key wildcard:

js
app.get('/files/*', (req, res) => {
  res.json({ path: req.params.wildcard });
});
PatternRequestreq.params.wildcard
/files/*/files/a/b/c.txt'a/b/c.txt'
/files/*/files/''
*/anything/at/all'anything/at/all'

A bare * route is the usual single-page-app or catch-all fallback, and is matched with the lowest priority because it is registered last:

js
app.get('*', (req, res) => res.sendFile('dist/index.html'));

How a path is compiled#

Patterns are compiled to a RegExp once, at registration, and reused for every request. compile(pattern, end) in src/router.js normalises the leading and trailing slashes, splits on :name and *, regex-escapes the literals, and turns :name into ([^/]+) and * into (.*).

text
/users/:id     end → /^\/users\/([^/]+)\/?$/     exact
/files/*       end → /^\/files\/(.*)\/?$/        exact
/api  (mount)  end → /^\/api(?=\/|$)/            prefix
/              end → /^\/?$/    prefix → /^/

Two details matter:

  • Routes use an exact match that tolerates a trailing slash (^…/?$).
  • Mounted middleware uses a prefix match with a lookahead (^…(?=/|$)), so /api matches /api and /api/users but not /apis.

Matching is case-sensitive: /Users and /users are different paths.

The captured names are stored in a keys array alongside the regex, and zipped back onto the match at request time, so parameter order is preserved.

Mounted routers#

A Router is a self-contained stack you can mount on a path:

js
import { App, Router } from 'routiva';

const api = new Router();
api.get('/status', (req, res) => res.json({ status: 'ok' }));

const app = new App();
app.use('/api', api);

app.use('/api', api) mounts the router at the /api prefix. When a request reaches it, the prefix is stripped before the inner router runs, so the router above sees /status, not /api/status — exactly like an Express sub-app. The original req.path, req.url, req.params and req.route are saved and restored the moment the mounted layer calls next(), so an outer route can continue where the inner router left off.

Routers nest: mount a router inside a router, and each prefix is stripped and restored in turn.

js
const admin = new Router();
admin.get('/users', (req, res) => res.json({ scope: 'admin' }));

const v1 = new Router();
v1.use('/admin', admin);          // /v1/admin/users

app.use('/v1', v1);

router.route()#

Register several methods for one path with a chainable builder:

js
app.route('/items')
  .get(listItems)
  .post(createItem)
  .delete(clearItems);

The chain exposes get, post, put, patch, delete, head, options and all, and every call returns the chain so calls can be stacked.

router.param()#

param(name, fn) registers a callback that runs whenever name appears in a matched route's parameters, before that route's handlers:

js
import { HttpError } from 'routiva';

app.param('id', (req, res, next, id, name) => {
  if (!/^\d+$/.test(id)) {
    return next(new HttpError(400, `${name} must be numeric`));
  }
  req.userId = Number(id);
  next();
});

app.get('/users/:id', (req, res) => {
  res.json({ id: req.userId });   // already validated and coerced
});
ArgumentMeaning
req, resThe wrapped request and response
nextContinue to the route handler, or next(err) to fail
valueThe decoded parameter value
nameThe parameter name

Callbacks are looked up on the router that registered the route, so a mounted router's params use its own callbacks. They run in parameter-name order, and a next(err) from any of them short-circuits straight to the error chain.

HEAD, OPTIONS and 405#

routiva handles the request-method corners of HTTP for you:

  • HEAD is served by a matching GET route. Headers (including Content-Length) are computed as usual; the body is suppressed.
  • OPTIONS on a known path is answered automatically with 204 and an Allow header listing the allowed methods.
  • A path that matches but a method that does not produces 405 Method Not Allowed with the same Allow header — not a 404.

The allowed list is recorded while the stack is scanned. When a GET route exists, HEAD is recorded with it, so a GET-only path reports Allow: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS.

http
OPTIONS /users HTTP/1.1

HTTP/1.1 204 No Content
Allow: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, POST

If you want to answer OPTIONS yourself, register a route for it; it matches before the built-in fallback. CORS middleware answers its own preflights too, which takes precedence — see CORS.

Registration order is execution order#

Routes and middleware share one ordered stack, so the first matching layer that responds wins. Register specific routes before catch-alls, and API routes before a static or SPA fallback:

js
app.get('/api/users', listUsers);              // matched first
app.use(serveStatic('public', { extensions: ['html'] }));
app.get('*', (req, res) => res.sendFile('dist/index.html'));  // last resort

A complete router#

js
import { App, Router, HttpError } from 'routiva';

const app = new App();

// Validate and coerce :id once for every route that uses it.
app.param('id', (req, res, next, id) => {
  if (!/^\d+$/.test(id)) return next(new HttpError(400, 'id must be numeric'));
  req.itemId = Number(id);
  next();
});

app.route('/items')
  .get((req, res) => res.json([]))
  .post((req, res) => res.status(201).json(req.body));

app.get('/items/:id', (req, res) => {
  res.json({ id: req.itemId });
});

app.get('/files/*', (req, res) => {
  res.json({ file: req.params.wildcard });
});

// Mounted sub-router, prefix stripped to "/v1"
const v1 = new Router();
v1.get('/ping', (req, res) => res.json({ pong: true }));
app.use('/v1', v1);

app.listen(3000);
